newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK gov't hails rail sale amid job cuts fear.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK gov't hails rail sale amid job cuts fear.

text.p: The British government hailed the end of the line for privatisation of the national rail network on Monday as five more private sector operators opened for business.
But the celebrations were marred by speculation of another 1,155 industry job cuts.
Rail operator chiefs tried to damp down redundancy rumours, saying nothing had been decided yet.

The issue has become sensitive in recent weeks since Stagecoach Holdings Plc dismissed many drivers at its South West Trains franchise -- a move which has led to scores of train cancellations and make it liable to the first fine by the industry regulator.
Transport minister Sir George Young said the government was now close to moving all of the 25 regional passenger rail franchises into private hands, signalling the end of railways privatisation.
"That process has been a remarkable success, with private operators pledged to new investment, extra services and lower subsidy from the taxpayer," he said.
All the franchises have now been awarded and the final private operators are expected to be running by the end of this month.
The sale of the 25 franchises follows the flotation of the rail infrastructure group Railtrack Plc and the three rolling stock leasing companies.

But the pressure group Save Our Railways (SOR) said it had evidence that two more rail operators were planning 1,155 job cuts. SOR said it had evidence that Regional Railways North West and Merseyrail planned job cuts of 800 and 355 respectively.
If this was mirrored nationwide, the rail industry would lose between 12,000 and 19,000 jobs as a result of privatisation, said SOR.

The plans by Regional Railways North West were revealed in leaked minutes of a meeting held by the Merseyside Passenger Transport Authority, it said. The meeting was held before the Great Western company had been formally awared the franchise.

The document, released by SOR, said Great Western "anticipate a massive redundancy within the existing workforce of 25 percent and in the opinion of this Authority this puts at risk services and has a huge social cost".

But John Sellers, the finance director of Great Western, denied it had already earmarked 800 jobs for the chop. "It is too early to tell what will happen. There has been no decision on job losses at present," said Sellers. But he conceded that he would be looking for cost savings.
Great Western is 51 percent owned by existing staff, with the remaining stake split between venture capital group 3i Plc and FirstBus Plc.

SOR also said it had documents showing that MTL Ltd, a Liverpool transport group, planned 355 job cuts at Merseyrail. MTL said in a statement it had "no contractual commitment to reduce jobs by any specific number" but did not rule out such a scenario.
A spokesman for the franchising regulator Opraf said most of the franchise bidders had built cost savings into their bids, which could mean job cuts.

But he warned that any repetition of the Stagecoach nightmare of cancelled trains and huge delays would lead to fines. "For every peak train which is cancelled we would impose a fine of 600 to 700 pounds," he said.
Opraf said the fine for Stagecoach, which has cancelled dozens of trains, could run to tens of thousands of pounds.

The franchising watchdog said that privatisation had been good for passengers, meaning more investment in trains, stations and security. Overall delays fell 30 percent in the six months to December 1996 compared with 1995.
But passenger bodies remain sceptical about Opraf's ability to monitor issues like train overcrowding and say the fines are too small to hurt errant operators.

SOR spokesman Jonathon Bray said: "Stagecoach gets millions of pounds in (government) subsidy a month and makes tens of millions in profits as a group. So tens of thousands of pounds in fines is peanuts."
